summary:
Chile's national framework applies in the Aysén region. Legal gender recognition has operated on a self-determination basis since 2019 under Gender Identity Law 21.120, with no medical or surgical conditions; same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022; the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences since 2012; and birth certificates have offered a third sex option since 2006. The Outright International Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, carries no Aysén-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding, so a visitor's expectations in the region rest on national law and national case data.

Recorded abuse in Aysén is rising. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) places the region at 0.65% of nationally documented abuse cases in 2025, a 25% increase year on year. The report cautions that a share of this size reflects weaker local documentation and safety infrastructure rather than low risk.

The national direction is the same and steeper. Movilh records 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest total in 24 years. Only Valparaíso and Metropolitana recorded a fall; the other 14 regions rose, a shift Movilh reads as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate around LGBTIQ+ rights. Aysén belongs to that rising group.

The rollback is legislative and budgetary as well as statistical. In the 2025-26 cycle the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children.
tangentialFactors:
Aysén's 0.65% share of nationally documented abuse cases in 2025 is small in absolute terms, but it is one of 14 regional shares moving upward while only Valparaíso and Metropolitana declined. Movilh's reading of the pattern is that reported hatred is spreading into regions where LGBTIQ+ rights receive less public discussion, which makes a low regional share an unreliable indicator of safety for a trans visitor.

The region's +25% year-on-year increase is slower than the national +27.1%, yet both sit within the same record-setting year: 2025 produced 23% of all discrimination cases documented over the past 24 years.

Chile's protections remain among the stronger ones in the region in statutory terms, while the policy record has stalled. The exclusion of the Gender Identity Support Program from the 2026 budget follows an assessment by a Chilean advocacy group that 2024 was the first year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights since the return of democracy in 1990, and Movilh's 2025 report describes a breakdown of consensus around those rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.
localsOnly:
Residents of Aysén access legal gender recognition, marriage, adoption and hate-crime aggravation through the national framework, with no regional statute of their own; the Outright International dossier records no region-specific legal or enforcement provision.

The defunding of the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget is a resident-facing loss of support infrastructure, and it was opposed by civil society organisations and the national ombuds for children rather than accepted without challenge.

Regional case volume is tracked in Movilh's national table, where Aysén accounted for 0.65% of documented abuse cases in 2025 after a 25% rise on 2024. The report treats this as a measure of how much abuse is being documented locally, not of how little occurs.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Aysén-specific incident, prosecution, detention-protocol or enforcement finding appears in the Outright International Chile dossier published 12 March 2026, and none is sourced here. Whether the Gendarmería de Chile trans-detention protocol has been implemented in the region's facilities is unresolved in this inventory.

The 2024 regional share of national cases is not reproduced in the 2025 edition of Movilh's report, so the two-year comparison for Aysén cannot be verified from the sources in hand; only the 2025 figure of 0.65% and the stated +25% change are sourced.

Whether Aysén's 0.65% share reflects lower incidence or lower reporting capacity is not resolved by the available material. Movilh's warning points toward the second reading, but the report does not quantify under-reporting by region.

No sourced data covers regional access to gender-affirming healthcare, identity-document processing times in Aysén, or hate-crime case outcomes within the region.
